name: Wei Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three mornings a week I'm in anatomy and exercise science, and the other two are practical sessions where we learn to assess a knee or a shoulder. I live in a shared flat with two guys on my course, and we cook in rotation. I work Saturdays at a sports shop, fitting running shoes. My parents run a bakery in the town where I grew up, so I also get a text every Sunday asking if I've eaten properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the practical sessions most, because you learn by putting your hands on somebody and being told you've got it wrong. What wears me out is the early starts and the amount to memorise. I've never been good at cramming, so I write things out three times, old-fashioned, and I don't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years someone announces that a new machine will change everything, and mostly it changes a few forms and a few spreadsheets. I'd say it at the shop, and my manager would nod, because the till system is the same one he's had for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I expected, so I'd feel no different. Physio is hands-on, and people don't want a chatbot putting a cold pack on their knee. My worries stay the usual ones: whether there are enough placements, and how many graduates compete for each physio job in my area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep my Saturday job, I'd keep up with the course, and I'd put some of my shop money aside for the second-year placement costs. I'd also ask my tutor which clinics take students in the holidays. I'm not changing anything in my life because of a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normal. Maybe a bit bored by the question, if I'm honest. This is the world I already live in, so no big feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has your family business seen any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the physiotherapy clinics near me started using software to book, assess and write notes, and hiring fewer people, I'd change my mind. Until I see that in a real clinic, I don't move. I've seen too many hyped things that didn't last. My dad says the same about new ovens, and he's usually right.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**: new machines mostly change a few forms and spreadsheets.
I'd shrug at the sports shop, where the till is the **same** as ten years ago.
think: Physio is **hands-on**, and nobody wants a chatbot putting a cold pack on their knee.
My real worries are **placements** and how many graduates compete for each local job.
do: **Keep** the Saturday shoe-fitting job and keep up with the course.
**Put** some shop money aside for second-year placement costs.
**Ask** my tutor which clinics take students in the holidays.
feel: **Normal**, maybe a bit bored by the question.
S0.quote: Until I see that in a real clinic, I don't move. I've seen too many hyped things that didn't last.
fieldNote: Wei is **genuinely unbothered**; his work is hands-on and his family help is steady.
He sets a **clear trigger** for changing his mind: seeing it in a real clinic.
His scepticism is **inherited**, with his dad's oven comparison.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday job fitting running shoes
Put shop wages aside for placement costs
Ask my tutor which clinics take students in the holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see who's right in a few years. I'd probably say the paperwork side of healthcare will shrink, and the patient side will stay. At the shop, I'd expect the ordering and the stock checks to go to software, and the person fitting your shoes to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think physio is mostly safe, but the clinic's front office and my future bookkeeping and note-taking could change. I might even like that, since I hate writing patient notes. What I'd worry about is clinics hiring fewer new graduates because each physio gets more done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my usual habits and try one new thing, but only if my tutor says it's proven. For example, I'd try the note-taking software on placement if the clinic uses it. I wouldn't go looking for tools. I'd also build my hands-on skills and my reputation, because patients choose a person they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more alert than before, but not worried. I'd say it's like hearing that the weather will change next year: I'll check the forecast, not cancel the holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about their bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about their bakery?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you draw the line on using these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep the shop as it is and look at the ordering side. Mum does the books by hand on Sunday nights, so a good program could save her five hours. They'd resist, because the bakery has worked for thirty years. I'd tell my parents it's the till and the books that change, not the bread.

say: I'd say the **paperwork** side of healthcare will shrink and the patient side will stay.
I'd expect shop ordering and stock checks to go to software, not the **person** fitting shoes.
think: Physio is mostly safe, and I'd be glad to lose **patient notes**, which I hate.
I'd worry clinics **hire fewer** graduates because each physio gets more done.
do: **Try** note-taking software on placement, but only if the clinic uses it.
**Build** hands-on skills and a reputation, because patients choose someone they trust.
**Keep** my usual routines and not go hunting for tools.
feel: **Alert**, but not worried, like checking a forecast rather than cancelling a holiday.
S1.quote: I'd tell my parents it's the till and the books that change, not the bread.
fieldNote: Wei keeps his **resistant** stance: he tries a tool only when forced by a workplace.
He is calm because his work is **hands-on** and his parents' bakery is low exposure.
The line about the **bread** is typical of his dry, concrete style.

steps.text: Use the clinic's note-taking software only if placement requires it
Practise hands-on assessment skills with course mates weekly
Suggest a bookkeeping program to my parents for the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a very short time to be certain about anything, and I'd say I'd want to see it happen before deciding. But I'd also say the government should have a plan, and I'd ask what the plan is, because nobody seems to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately this one hits me. If thinking work is done by 2028, office jobs would go. People on office salaries are the ones who buy bread from my parents' bakery and pay for physio. I'd be in my third year, and clinics might not hire if patients cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about whether they've got savings if sales fall. I'd keep my shop job and add a second weekend shift. I'd stay with the physio degree, because the hands-on part is what lasts until 2031. And I'd ask my tutors which parts of the course are hardest for a machine, and focus on those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. I keep it in, like a clenched hand. I'd be short with my flatmates and I'd go for long runs to clear my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the bakery's situation change what you'd do with your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Does the bakery's situation change what you'd do with your degree?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd probably want to finish quicker and start earning, even if I can't do everything I want. If the bakery hit trouble, I'd need to send money home, not take it. I'd move back in with them if I had to, and drive in for lectures. I'd hate it, but I'd do it for them.

say: I'd say two years is too short to be **certain** and I'd want to see it happen first.
I'd ask the government for a **plan**, because nobody seems to know one.
think: People on office salaries buy my parents' **bread**, so their jobs matter to the bakery.
I'd be in my third year when clinics might **stop hiring**.
do: **Ask** my parents what savings the bakery has if sales fall.
**Add** a second weekend shift at the sports shop.
**Focus** on the course's hardest hands-on skills for a machine.
feel: **Tense**, like a clenched hand, so I'd go for long runs.
S2.quote: People on office salaries are the ones who buy bread from my parents' bakery and pay for physio.
fieldNote: Wei's worry is **second-order**: customers' incomes, then the bakery, then his own clinic jobs.
He would **go home** to help if the bakery failed, which shows loyalty over self-interest.
He asks for a **government plan** but does not expect one.

steps.text: Ask my parents what savings the bakery has
Take a second weekend shift at the sports shop
Spend extra hours on hands-on physio techniques
Write to my councillor asking for a plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years sounds like the kind of promise people make to get attention, but I'd listen. I'd say the sensible thing is for every business, even small ones, to look at what they could do without a person and what they couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better than in the two-year version. I'd finish in 2029 and have two years of working before anything hands-on is replaced. And a physio's job still needs a body on the table. I'd just want to be good enough that patients ask for me by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and start in a busy clinic where I'd see many patients. I'd save as much as I could so I'd have a cushion by the time robots arrive. I'd help my parents think about a second income for the bakery, like selling online or catering for offices. I'd still wait to see before buying any tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A knot in the stomach on bad days, but I'd probably be training and not thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you still wait to see on the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you still wait to see on the tools?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your parents' bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because most of them are expensive and half of them don't work properly. If one of them was clearly saving my colleagues time, I'd adopt it. I don't mind being second. Being second means someone else has already found the bugs, and that's a decent place to be.

say: I'd say five years sounds like a promise to get **attention**, but I'd listen.
I'd say every business should list what it could do without a **person**.
think: I'd work for **two years** before anything hands-on is replaced.
A physio's job still needs a **body on the table**, so I'd aim to be asked for by name.
do: **Start** in a busy clinic to see many patients and build a name.
**Save** as much as possible for a cushion before robots arrive.
**Help** my parents add online orders or office catering to the bakery.
feel: **Steady**, with a knot in the stomach on bad days.
S3.quote: I don't mind being second. Being second means someone else has already found the bugs, and that's a decent place to be.
fieldNote: His **resistance** is a strategy: be second so others find the bugs.
The time gap lets him **plan for the bakery** instead of panicking.
Mood is uneasy because the **customer base** of the family bakery stays exposed.

steps.text: Take a first job at a busy clinic to see many patients
Save a third of my first salary
Help my parents set up online orders and office catering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to see what actually works, so let's not make big decisions on guesses. I'd say it, and then get on with my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, a qualified physio, and probably running my own small practice or sharing one. Hands-on work would be the last to change, and by then I'd have savings. My parents would be close to retiring the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my degree and a couple of years in a clinic. Then I'd move towards my own practice, perhaps with a partner. I'd keep an eye on what machines can do in rehab, and I'd adopt the ones that help my patients. I'd save more than I spend, and I'd help my parents plan a sale or a handover to a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is a long time to hold your breath, and I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a handover of the bakery look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a handover of the bakery look like?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably selling to a younger baker who wants to keep the name. Mum would be sad and Dad would act like he isn't. I'd help with the paperwork. I'm not a baker, and I never wanted to be, but I'd want the shop to carry on in someone's hands.

say: I'd say a decade is long enough to see **what works**, so don't decide on guesses.
I'd say it once and then **get on** with my life.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, a qualified **physio**, maybe in my own practice.
Hands-on work should change **last**, and my parents would be near retiring the bakery.
do: **Work** two years in a clinic, then aim for a shared private practice.
**Adopt** rehab machines only once they clearly help patients.
**Help** my parents plan a bakery sale or a handover.
feel: **Calm**; a decade is too long to hold your breath.
S4.quote: A decade is a long time to hold your breath, and I won't.
fieldNote: Wei's calm in S4 is **earned by time** and hands-on work, not by denial.
He plans to be an **adopter after proof**, never a pioneer.
He sees **handover** as the kind of family duty he accepts.

steps.text: Work two years in a busy clinic after graduating
Save more than I spend from my first salary
Plan a bakery handover with my parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because a lot of people would be hit before they can adjust, including the customers my parents rely on. What would help is clear information from my university about which clinics hire, and a real plan from the government for workers who lose their jobs. And honest advice, not hype either way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being sceptical isn't the same as being asleep. I just want proof before I change my life, and I think a lot of people feel that.

headlineQuote: Being sceptical isn't the same as being asleep. I just want proof before I change my life
portrait: Wei is **nineteen**, a first-year physiotherapy student who works Saturdays fitting running shoes and shares a flat.
He is a **centrist** and resistant to new technology, never uses AI tools and waits for proof first.
His parents run a small bakery, so his worry is **customers' incomes** more than his own work.
He stays calm in slow worlds and becomes **anxious** only when AGI arrives within two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, hitting customers of his parents' bakery before anyone can adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information about which clinics **hire**, plus a real government plan for workers who lose jobs.
